title: Age Friendly Inventory and Campus Climate Survey (ICCS)
purpose: To provide campuses with tools to evaluate age-friendly practices, perceptions of inclusivity, and areas for improvement using a systematic, campus-wide approach.
outcomes: Universities can identify existing age-inclusive practices and gaps. Data supports decision-making for policy, programming, and campus culture. Provides evidence-based priorities for advancing age inclusivity.
unique: It is one of the first standardized tools that combines both an inventory of practices and a climate survey to capture perceptions, giving a full picture of age inclusivity on campus.
type: One-Time Activity (I.e., pedagogical ideas, specific activities, or trips)
challenges: Securing buy-in from faculty and administrators for wide participation. Ensuring surveys capture diverse perspectives across large campuses. Need for resources to analyze and act on results.

title: Musicians in Residence Program at Mirabella at ASU
purpose: To provide an immersive, intergenerational program where students and older adults collaborate through music, dance, and creative arts, building meaningful relationships that support lifelong learning, community connection, and cultural engagement.
outcomes: Built strong intergenerational bonds between students and older adults through weekly performances. Provided Mirabella residents with free or reduced-price access to ASU cultural events. Created opportunities for residents to join ensembles such as choral groups, guitar groups, and jazz ensembles, participating directly alongside ASU students. Earned external recognition, including the 2023 Innovation Award from Arizona Leading Age and an honorable mention in the 2022 Mather Institute Promising Practices Awards. Served as a deciding factor older adults to move into Mirabella, since the program shows ASU’s commitment to lifelong learning and community building.
unique: This is a fully immersive intergenerational residency where ASU graduate students live at Mirabella and co-create music, dance, and arts programming with residents. The “flex engagement” model lets residents shape activities, fostering mutual benefit and strong community ties.
type: Ongoing Activity (I.e., events that occur yearly, structural changes in operations))
challenges: long-term funding and institutional support, balancing graduate students’ academic responsibilities with the program’s immersive demands. Ensuring accessibility for residents with varied levels of prior artistic or musical training and expanding programming to include diverse art forms while maintaining quality and resident engagement.

title: Trent University Intergenerational Classroom
purpose: Dr. Elizabeth Russell and Tabytha Wells developed, implemented, and evaluated an intergenerational Psychology of Aging course at Trent University in Winter, 2024 and 2026. This third-year course included and intentionally connected 60 university students and 13 older participants from the community (aged 65+). The classroom aimed to encourage a diverse view of aging while fostering meaningful intergenerational connections through formal lectures and informal intergenerational group activities.
outcomes: 2 iterations of an intergenerational psychology of aging classroom have happened
unique: Older adults are fully integrated into the classroom space across the entire course, and the special weekly small-group intergenerational activities that we do
type: Ongoing Activity (I.e., events that occur yearly, structural changes in operations))
challenges: sustainable funding, too much interest from the community vs. the spaces that we can accommodate in the course

title: Micro-certificate – Facilitating Older Adult Learning
purpose: The main goal of this micro-certificate is to provide an educational opportunity for a wide range of individuals who might work or volunteer in any kind of setting where older adults are learning. Within the micro-certificate there are three courses of 4 weeks each: 1) Older Adult Development and Long Life; 2) Universal Design for Learning to Facilitate Older Adult Learning; and 3) Using Technology for Teaching and Learning with Older Adults.
outcomes: The first offering was well received with positive reviews. You can see testimonial videos on the website. There was a second offering, but the enrolment was lower.
unique:
This online learning opportunity is available to Canadian and international students. While it has specific time frames, it is offered asynchronously so it can suit people who may have many other responsibilities.

It also conveys that learning by older adults can occur in many different settings beyond formal learning environments.
type: Ongoing Activity (I.e., events that occur yearly, structural changes in operations))
challenges:
•	Although this micro-certificate is a non-credit offering (i.e., not towards a degree), it still requires many difficult steps for registration (e.g., transcripts).
•	Because this is offered through Extended Education, the fees are relatively high, as costs are not subsidized.
•	These issues challenge being able to offer it.

title: Consulting with Senior Scholars and Professors Emeriti
purpose: We consulted with Deans, Senior Scholars and Professors Emeriti, to find out what practices and experiences are for retirees who hold unpaid academic appointments with the University. Based on findings and recommendations, many policies, procedures and initiatives are occurring for individuals in these positions and all retirees of the University.
outcomes: Much more information is available for prospective retirees. Better engagement of Senior Scholars and Professors Emeriti and feelings that they are valued. Strategic funding from University to pilot many new initiatives.
unique: First time that our University has ever consulted with these retirees. Recommendations are geared to a world affected by the pandemic and the new ways of working and engaging. Although this work focused on retirees there are other aspects of the University which will be positively impacted.
type: One-Time Activity (I.e., pedagogical ideas, specific activities, or trips)
challenges:
Because we had champions at some of the highest levels in the University this project has gone quite smoothly with buy-in from Deans and others. 

We are also conducting a consultation with all retirees (faculty and staff) to learn more about engagement and connection with the University.

title: Grant funding competition for Age-Friendly University initiatives
purpose: The primary purpose was to ensure that more units (academic and non-academic) at the University were engaging in activities to improve the age-friendliness of the university. In addition, the competition presented an opportunity to build awareness at the University about AFU principles. And finally, funded groups learned from each other.
outcomes: Four AFU projects were completed that likely never would have happened without the funding. Units involved included Extended Education, Architectural and Engineering Services, the School of Art Gallery, and Alumni Relations. Projects involved creating a micro-certificate, campus wayfinding, an inter-generational artist series, and technology training courses.
unique: By engaging directly with all four groups on a monthly basis, they were able to support each and learn from AFU experts. The initiative showed that other units without aging experience can engage in projects, but they likely need support from those with gerontological experience.
type: One-Time Activity (I.e., pedagogical ideas, specific activities, or trips)
challenges: Some projects did not carry over beyond project completion in meaningful ways, but all groups are now much more aware of how to think about including older individuals in the work that they do.

title: University of Manitoba Cicero Club
purpose: Collegial support for older adult students (age 50+). Members network and confront the challenges that they face at university. As Mallman and Lee write, One cannot know how “marginalized and detached from student networks of sociality and information an older student can be simply by virtue of age.” Members work to create a truly age-friendly university environment. As educator Muni Abdi argues, “It is not inclusion if you invite people into a space you are not willing to change.”
outcomes: Students who had given up are graduating, new friendships are lasting beyond graduation—even graduates are attending the meetings—and mental health has been supported. The UMCC has also participated in intergenerational panels such as Students Targeting Aging Research (STAR).
unique: Although The University of Manitoba had endorsed the 10 charter principles of Age-Friendly University, there was no dedicated club for this worthy demographic.
type: Ongoing Activity (I.e., events that occur yearly, structural changes in operations))
challenges: Recruitment, attrition due to graduation, meeting times and space, financial aid

title: University Student Organization, "Senior Scholars at USF" is a senior citizen-led group.

We are dedicated to empowering lifelong learners to participate actively, purposefully, and meaningfully in all aspects of campus life—academically, socially, and culturally. We strive to integrate senior-focused perspectives into USF's broader academic and administrative framework.
outcomes: We have helped our seniors register for classes, develop social connections, and become aware the benefits the University provides for them. Additionally, we have worked with upper university management to remove course enrollment obstacles presented by some professors.
unique: We are an official Student Organization.
type: One-Time Activity (I.e., pedagogical ideas, specific activities, or trips)
challenges: Reaching a large percentage of seniors on campus. Most seniors only take a class or two during any given semester.

outcomes:

title: World Human Rights Cities Forum 2026: “AI, Well-Aging and Human Rights”
purpose: The forum's primary purpose is to reframe "well-aging" as a human-rights issue in the era of AI and digital transformation, and to build regional governance dialogue on the digital divide, exclusion, and fundamental rights of older adults. It links Gwangju's human-rights city vision with Chosun University's well-aging research to advance a human-centered model of digital inclusion, convening the university, local government, civil society, and international organizations to translate dialogue into regional action.
outcomes: 191 attendees: 38 faculty/staff, 132 students (44 Korean, 88 international), and 21 external guests including UN OHCHR officers. Held as Chosun University's special session within the World Human Rights Cities Forum hosted by Gwangju Metropolitan City, the forum declared the "Jeonnam-Gwangju Digital Inclusion and Well-Aging Implementation Plan," setting four action tasks: ethical AI design, universal digital access, community connection, and a sustainable well-aging ecosystem. A standing cooperation network among the university, local government, civil society, and the UN was established, turning the declaration into an ongoing regional agenda for older adults' digital rights.
unique: It uniquely connects three worlds rarely brought together: a UN human-rights body (OHCHR), human-rights city (Gwangju), and a university's well-aging research. By framing aging not as welfare but as a digital-rights issue, it positions older adults as rights-holders, and turned dialogue into a signed regional implementation plan.
type: Ongoing Activity (I.e., events that occur yearly, structural changes in operations))
challenges: Recruiting domestic and international speakers who simultaneously cover AI, human rights, and well-aging was difficult, as the convergence pool is limited. Internal budget rules also constrained honoraria for foreign experts. Going forward, we plan to expand access to aging experts through exchange and partnerships with AFU member universities.

title: Well-Aging Senior Life Care Program ‘Art Walk’
purpose: To support healthy, active aging by giving local seniors (aged 50+) hands-on access to the arts at a university-run urban campus art center. Over 15 sessions, participants learn art theory, practice, and creation step by step—many exhibiting their own work for the first time—turning art into a lasting hobby and means of self-expression. The program also builds a sustainable well-aging culture by connecting Chosun University, Dong-gu District, and local artists with the community.
outcomes: Fifteen local seniors completed the first round of the program, taking part in 15 sessions from December 16, 2025 to February 3, 2026. Their works were presented at a closing exhibition at the campus art center on February 3, 2026, marking the first time many participants had ever exhibited their own art. One participant shared that she was so deeply moved by seeing her work on display that she almost cried. Participant satisfaction reached 95 out of 100 (13 respondents). The program drew local media coverage as a university-led model for senior cultural engagement, and a second, advanced-level round is planned for 2026 to deepen participants' artistic development.
unique: Participant feedback showed each two-hour session felt too short to cover theory and practice. The twice-a-week schedule also created attendance burdens, leading to mid-term cancellations. The first round focused mainly on painting, with limited exploration into design and convergent art. Maintaining attendance and diversity remains a challenge.
type: Ongoing Activity (I.e., events that occur yearly, structural changes in operations))
challenges: Participant feedback showed each two-hour session felt too short to cover theory and practice. The twice-a-week schedule also created attendance burdens, leading to mid-term cancellations. The first round focused mainly on painting, with limited exploration into design and convergent art. Maintaining attendance and diversity remains a challenge.

title: Age-Inclusive Guide for Higher Education
purpose: This introductory guide promotes age-inclusive thinking and practice within higher education. It serves as a starting point for reflection, conversation, and ongoing learning among those at universities and colleges who engage with age-diverse students, faculty, and staff.
outcomes: The guide has been shared across the institution and has received positive feedback from members of the campus community. Two summaries of key content have also been developed to supplement the guide. Anticipated outcomes include increased understanding of aging, ageism, and age-inclusive practices, as well as the integration of these practices across campus contexts.
unique: The guide provides foundational knowledge of aging and ageism, along with practical strategies for applying age-inclusive practices across key areas of higher education.
duration: The guide was developed from June 2025 to May 2026.
type: One-Time Activity (I.e., pedagogical ideas, specific activities, or trips)
challenges: Balancing diverse perspectives of pilot readers and determining the appropriate scope/detail to provide an introduction while supporting self-directed learning. Potential uptake challenges include perceptions that age inclusivity is not a priority, not relevant to one’s role, or is outside one’s influence, and difficulty engaging leadership.

outcomes: None

title: UNI~COM: Lifelong Learning
purpose: UNI~COM: Lifelong Learning is a voluntary, university-hosted organization for individuals 50 and over — retired, semi-retired, or still employed. It offers non-credit study groups, speaker luncheons, and cultural programs designed to foster intellectual engagement, social connection, and continued learning in a university setting, without exams or academic prerequisites.
outcomes: Nearly 200 participants annually; 10 courses offered in Winter 2025. Activities have included museum and cultural site visits (Detroit Institute of Art, Toledo Museum of Art), speaker luncheons, and study groups. Profits are donated to the University of Windsor Bursary Fund (e.g., $5,000 in 2017).
unique: Open to anyone 50+ regardless of university affiliation — not limited to retirees or alumni. Combines academic-style study groups with cultural excursions and social luncheons, and reinvests proceeds directly into student bursaries, linking older-adult learning to student support.
type: Ongoing Activity (I.e., events that occur yearly, structural changes in operations))
challenges: Nil
